content:
“I gotta say, my dad was a pretty gifted guy. I wish he would have used it in a different way. But he (didn’t). And here we are.”

Clint Patterson offered this lament while he ruminated on his father Roger Patterson’s famous 1967 footage depicting a large, muscular, ape-like creature lumbering through rural Northern California. Dubbed the “Patterson-Gimlin Film,” the footage seemed to offer concrete evidence to a volatile conspiracy and brought financial turmoil to an entire town.

Nearly 60 years later, discovered rehearsal footage locked away in a vault may blow the whole story wide open. “It completely changes the source of the story around that film,” said director Marq Evans. In response, The Daily Californian sat down with Patterson, along with the filmmakers behind the documentary “Capturing Bigfoot,” to discuss exactly how much has changed with the team’s newly uncovered evidence.

While documentaries about Bigfoot are practically a dime a dozen, Evans and producer Tamir Ardon were shocked to find that no one had ever formally investigated the origin story of the pivotal footage which the creature’s existence largely rests upon. Ardon notes he and Evans “didn’t have any skin in the game,” as neither was particularly swayed by either side of the Bigfoot debate. That distance, he explains, let them approach the project “from a journalistic standpoint,” focusing on what they could prove with the new footage and what it meant for the group of small-town men involved. Evans puts it plainly: “We’re not speaking to the existence of Bigfoot or not, we’re just telling this one story.”

The story is also personal for Evans. He was born in Yakima, Washington, home to Roger Patterson, Bob Gimlin and, notably, Albert DeAtley — CEO of Superior Asphalt and patron to the cowboys behind the film. Growing up, he heard his father’s Bigfoot stories on camping trips: “His version of it was that Al DeAtley was the mastermind, and he wore this Bigfoot costume. So he had some things right. Most of it was wrong,” Evans recalled. “Which I’ve come to realize is true with almost everybody that talks about this subject. There’s a lot of misinformation out there, and for me, that started with the stories I heard from my dad.”

The experience shaped Evans’ search for the truth. “As a documentary filmmaker, you’re always after 100% truth, but there’s certainly this emotional component to it,” he said. “Werner Herzog calls it the ecstatic truth versus the accountant’s truth. The accountant’s truth is just straight facts. But that is often not as true as that ecstatic truth or the emotional truth.”

That pursuit creates a tension in the film. Seeking an absolute truth about a legend built on very little hard evidence means confronting the limits of what can be proven. Patterson, however, sees it more simply: “The truth doesn’t change, and it stays the same.”

That emotional truth ended up coming into focus through Patterson himself. “We actually had a 25-minute, very rough assembly prior to the interview with Clint, just based off archives and a few early interviews. I remember about one hour into the interview with Clint thinking, ‘Well, that 25-minute cut we have … that’s garbage. We’re starting over because Clint is now the main character.’ That became evident very fast,” Evans said. Ardon seconded this, adding that the film’s heart is the family journey: “You don’t have to care about Bigfoot to watch this film.”

Despite these intentions, the team knew it would be up against the vicious scrutiny of staunch believers and fervent deniers alike. “It’s the adult version of Santa Claus,” Ardon remarked, “The idea that there’s this mythical creature out there that's just kind of living their life on their own terms and not beholden to the laws and rules of civilization is something cool, and people don’t want to give that up, or be told that that might not exist.” Even so, Ardon says, unlike most conspiracy films, this one leaves viewers “with an actual ending.”

For Patterson, that resistance has been personal. He recalled, in both the interview and throughout the documentary, the rifts this footage, new and old, has caused in his own life. After the passing of his father, licensing the “Patterson-Gimlin Film” became the family’s main source of income, and Patterson’s mother feared that his participation in a documentary of this nature may ruin that nest egg, leading to her to disown him. Money runs through the whole story. “It’s a story of money and greed,” Patterson said, pointing to DeAtley, who saw a chance to make money and used it to “(save) his company.” Evans agreed: “I don’t think you can tell the Bigfoot story without the financial component.”

In a story about a mythical beast, it’s this human side of the story that is what stands out as so compelling. “Clint, you’re a documentarian’s dream,” Ardon said, prompting a shy smile to creep over his face. “He’d be proud of us,” Patterson says, referring to his father. “He’d be proud of what we’ve done.”
